items.readable_text:
Content:
The power rule for exponents states that a power raised to another power is equal to the product of the two powers:

Content:
[MATH: \left(a^m\right)^n = a^{mn}]

Content:
For example,

Content:
[MATH: \eqalign{
\left(5^2\right)^3 &= \
5^{2 \cdot 3} &= \
5^6.
}]

Content:
To see why the power rule for exponents is true, let's take the above example and work it out again, the long way:

Content:
[MATH: \eqalign{
\left(5^2\right)^3 &= \[5pt]
\underbrace{5^2\cdot 5^2\cdot 5^2}_{3\text{ times}} &= \[5pt]
(5 \cdot 5) \cdot (5 \cdot 5) \cdot (5 \cdot 5) &= \[5pt]
\underbrace{5\cdot5\cdot5\cdot5\cdot5\cdot5}_{6\text{ times}} &= \[5pt]
5^6
}]

Content:
The power rule for exponents is just a shortcut for the process above.

items.readable_text:
Content:
Suppose we want to remove the radical term in an expression like [MATH: \sqrt{x^{3}}.] To do this, we first convert the radical to a fractional exponent:

Content:
[MATH: \sqrt{x^{3}}= \left(x^{3}\right)^{1/2}]

Content:
Then, we can apply the power rule and multiply the fractional exponents:

Content:
[MATH: (x^{3})^{1/2}|=; x^{(3) ⋅ (1/2)}|=; x^{3/2}]

Content:
Therefore,

Content:
[MATH: \sqrt{x^{3}} = x^{3/2},]

Content:
and in general,

Content:
[MATH: \sqrt[n]{x^m} = x^{m/n}.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
The power rule for exponents states that a power raised to another power is equal to the product of the two powers:

Content:
[MATH: \left(a^m\right)^n = a^{mn}]

Content:
For example,

Content:
[MATH: \eqalign{
\left(5^2\right)^3 &= \
5^{2 \cdot 3} &= \
5^6.
}]

Content:
To see why the power rule for exponents is true, let's take the above example and work it out again, the long way:

Content:
[MATH: \eqalign{
\left(5^2\right)^3 &= \[5pt]
\underbrace{5^2\cdot 5^2\cdot 5^2}_{3\text{ times}} &= \[5pt]
(5 \cdot 5) \cdot (5 \cdot 5) \cdot (5 \cdot 5) &= \[5pt]
\underbrace{5\cdot5\cdot5\cdot5\cdot5\cdot5}_{6\text{ times}} &= \[5pt]
5^6
}]

Content:
The power rule for exponents is just a shortcut for the process above.

Content:
and in general,

Content:
[MATH: \sqrt[n]{x^m} = x^{m/n}.]

Explanation:
First, we convert the radical to a fractional exponent, and then we apply the power rule:

[MATH: ((1)/(root(x, 3)))^{4} ⋅ x|=; ((1)/(x^{1/3}))^{4} ⋅ x|=; (x^{− 1/3})^{4} ⋅ x|=; x^{(− 1/3) ⋅ (4)} ⋅ x|=; x^{− 4/3} ⋅ x]

Finally, we apply the product rule, adding the exponents:

[MATH: x^{− 4/3} ⋅ x|=; x^{− 4/3} ⋅ x^{1}|=; x^{− 4/3 + 1}|=; x^{− 4/3 + 3/3}|=; x^{− 1/3}]

Therefore [MATH: k=-\dfrac{1}{3}.]
